title: GPU runtime profiling - kernel selection & TRT-LLM vs vLLM deep dive (NovaEdge)
summary: Deep technical session to review GPU runtime profiling results for NovaEdge: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graphs benefits, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization profiles, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed next steps: share benchmark spreadsheet, run 1-week pilot on dedicated nodes, scope quantization tests, and provide security docs for private deployment.
action_items: Olivia: share raw perf traces + filtered nvprof/cudaGraph logs (due 2026-12-14)
Ethan: provide representative prompt set and production seq length distribution (due 2026-12-13)
Samir: send pilot proposal and pricing for 4 dedicated A100 nodes (due 2026-12-16)
Priya: confirm network egress and KMS requirements for Private deployment (due 2026-12-15)
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet and runbook link
NovaEdge to provision pilot credentials and test data set
Schedule follow-up check-in after pilot results (2 weeks)

header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Olivia Chen (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood Perf Eng); Rachel Kim (NovaEdge CTO), Ethan Park (ML Infra Lead), Priya Singh (SRE), Alex Torres (Staff ML Eng)
Recording: available
Shared artifacts: deck + benchmark spreadsheet (internal links noted in transcript)
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanna focus today on the gpu runtime profiling results and kernel selection strategies, and then dig into the trt-llm vs vLLM tradeoffs, cuda graphs, plus your VPC/on-prem constraints
[00:12] Rachel: awesome, thanks Samir. quick context: we're trying to move inference for our assistant to dedicated infra, 8k token recs, high concurrency, need sub-200ms p95 for small prompts but tolerate higher for long sequences. security is key - KMS + private network.
[00:28] Olivia: noted; we brought Marcus today to go through traces and kernel selection logic. we'll start with the profiling summary then show a couple of flame graphs and the cudaGraph capture.
[00:40] Marcus: ok jumping in, slide 1 shows baseline runs: model = open-llama-30b varint, runs on A100-80GB; we compared three stacks: stock vLLM runtime, our TensorRT-LLM pipeline, and a hybrid where we use vLLM for scheduling but TRT kernels for matmuls. profiling was done with nvprof and also cuda-memcheck for correctness.
[01:05] Ethan: quick Q - did you warm the kv cache before measuring? in prod we have long prefixes that are cached so cold-start numbers aren't representative.
[01:12] Marcus: good call - we did both cold and hot runs; the spreadsheet (link in dropbox) has the numbers. cold runs show TRT-LLM faster on raw matmul time but vLLM scheduled batched attention has better latency for small batches because of less launch overhead. in hot runs where kv cache is primed, TRT-LLM's kernel fusion + cudagraphs wins at steady-state throughput.
[01:39] Alex: when you say kernel fusion, is that the tensorrt custom fused kernels or your own fused attention kernels?
[01:45] Olivia: mostly TRT fused kernels for attention and softmax+norm fusion, plus a layernorm/matmul fused path we instrumented. there are places where vLLM's open kernels have better memory locality at small seq lengths.
[02:00] [00:02:00] Rachel: ok do you have numbers for p50/p95 for our workload? average seq len ~480 tokens, but tail goes to 6k.
[02:12] Marcus: in the spreadsheet sheet 'novaedge_480' there's p50/p95. short summary: TRT-LLM + cudagraphs: p50 ~46ms p95 ~212ms for 480 tokens on 1 A100 for 1 request at a time; vLLM (default scheduling) p50 ~52ms p95 ~260ms. for longer seqs the delta shrinks because KV cache memory bandwidth dominates.
[02:40] Ethan: that p95 ~212ms is with cudagraphs enabled? we saw weird tail spikes when enabling cudagraphs intermittently in our tests.
[02:50] Marcus: yes it's with cudagraphs and kernel auto-replay warmup. tail spikes we saw too - often due to dynamic graph reinitialization when batch shapes change; cudagraphs are sensitive to shape polymorphism. we recommend shape bucketing to reduce recreations.
[03:07] Priya: can you explain more about shape bucketing? we'd prefer not to change app logic.
[03:13] Olivia: shape bucketing is transparent to the application - at runtime we group similar seq lengths into buckets and reuse a cached cudaGraph per bucket, so runtime only needs to pick the closest bucket. tradeoff: small amount of wasted compute for padding vs avoiding expensive graph recompile. we saw 10-15% p95 improvement after bucketing in mixed workloads.
[03:36] [00:03:36] Rachel: what about quantization? we're exploring int8/4-bit to reduce memory footprint to run more replicas. any quality regressions expected?
[03:46] Marcus: we ran a quantization sweep with PTQ and a small calibration set; 8-bit qlinear had ~0.3% perplexity increase, 4-bit groupwise dynamic showed ~1.8% perplexity increase. quality depends on model and prompt distribution; we recommend a small eval suite. we'll share the quantization config we used.
[04:07] Alex: did you test quantized kernels with TRT-LLM? some mixed precision kernels behave differently in TRT.
[04:13] Olivia: yes, TRT-LLM with FP16 + int8 matmul kernels gave best perf/quality tradeoff. pure 4-bit required extra calibration and sometimes bespoke kernels - it's doable but needs an extra engineering pass.
[04:27] Ethan: curious about KV cache management - we've seen memory fragmentation when caching many long conversations. what are your recommendations?
[04:35] Marcus: fragmentation often comes from per-request variable length caches and repeated allocations. our runtime pre-allocates large KV arenas and uses slab allocation; also supports eviction policies and prefix sharing across requests when safe. For NovaEdge we suggested a hybrid: keep last-N tokens per session and centralize long-term archives to CPU cold storage.
[04:56] Rachel: on the security front, what do you need for private deployment? we run in a VPC with KMS and strict egress rules.
[05:03] Samir: standard - we support customer-managed KMS/HSM, SAML SSO, RBAC, and can deploy a Private control plane in your VPC. For air-gapped on-prem we ship an appliance image; we need <list> of ports and an initial service account. We'll send the security pack after this call.
[05:21] Priya: ok please include audit log retention options and encryption-at-rest details.
[05:25] Samir: yes, will include SOC2/ISO artifacts and audit log config.
[05:30] [00:05:30] Alex: back to kernel selection - how does Redwood choose kernels at runtime? is it heuristics or an ML-based selector?
[05:38] Marcus: currently heuristics + cost model. we measure kernel latency per op shape and keep a profile catalog. when a shape appears we pick the lowest-cost kernel according to cost model (compute + memory + launch overhead). we also have an offline tuner that runs microbenchmarks to populate the catalog for a given hardware type.
[05:55] Rachel: does that adapt over time if hardware gets patched or different drivers affect performance?
[05:59] Marcus: yes, we version kernel profiles per driver/runtime combo. we detect large deviations and flag for retuning. for customers on Dedicated we recommend a periodic re-run of the tuner after driver updates.
[06:12] Ethan: have you compared scheduling approaches - vLLM's batching vs Redwood's continuous batching? any stability differences?
[06:20] Olivia: we did a head-to-head: vLLM's batching is great for latency when request sizes are homogenous and arrival rates are steady. Redwood continuous batching focuses on maximizing throughput while preserving p95 SLOs using adaptive time budgets; it performs better under bursty traffic. we included the arrival pattern traces in the spreadsheet.
[06:41] [00:06:41] Alex: regarding cudagraphs - can you elaborate on when to enable/disable? we saw reduced latency in steady-state but worse tail when workload is spiky.
[06:50] Marcus: right - enable cudagraphs when you have stable input shapes or use bucketing. disable or use short-lived graphs when you have highly variable shapes. additionally, pre-warming graphs during low traffic times reduces tail. we also have an auto-cudagraph mode that tracks graph recreation frequency and disables if recreations exceed threshold.
[07:10] Rachel: what's the integration effort if we want TRT kernels + Redwood runtime but keep our scheduler?
[07:16] Olivia: integration is a couple of steps: you can plugin our TRT kernel library with minimal changes, or we can run a hybrid mode where vLLM scheduler calls into our fused kernels. we have a sample repo and a helm chart for Dedicated. we'll share an integration guide.
[07:30] Ethan: does Redwood collect telemetry from on-prem deployments? we have strict PII rules.
[07:35] Samir: telemetry is opt-in; minimal heartbeats can be sent via a customer-controlled endpoint. logs can be kept locally and only hashed fingerprints shared for SLA debugging. we'll include exact telemetry schema in the security pack.
[07:50] [00:07:50] Alex: small point - we noticed in your slides a mention of hybrid TRT/vLLM giving the best of both worlds. can you walk a concrete path for our pilot?
[07:59] Marcus: suggestion: Pilot config = 4 A100 nodes, TRT kernels for attention+matmul, vLLM scheduler for dynamic batching, cudagraphs with 3 buckets (short/mid/long), FP16 + selective int8 on matmul, and KV arena preallocation. Run 1 week with production-like traffic. We'll instrument and share per-token cost and latency breakdowns.
[08:25] Priya: sounds good. we need to know the network topology and storage mounts for KV. will that be in the runbook?
[08:31] Olivia: yes, runbook includes required mounts, NFS vs local NVMe recommendations, and network egress ports. also notes on KMS and SSO.
[08:42] Rachel: any gotchas or known issues?
[08:45] Marcus: main things: cudagraphs + shape polymorphism, quantization needing careful calibration for 4-bit, and memory fragmentation if you don't pre-allocate arenas. also driver mismatches can cause perf regressions - stick to validated driver/kernel combos we provide in the runbook.
[08:59] [00:08:59] Samir: quick recap for next steps: Olivia will share traces and graphs; Samir will send pilot proposal and security pack; NovaEdge provides sample prompt set and infra contact; Marcus will prepare a quantization test plan.
[09:12] Rachel: agreed. one ask - can you include an estimate of cost per 1M tokens on the pilot config vs hosted option?
[09:18] Samir: yes I'll attach a cost estimate in the pilot email.
[09:22] Ethan: timeline expectation? we can start the pilot as early as next week if the onboarding is light.
[09:27] Samir: we can stand up pilot infra in 5 business days once credentials and order are approved.
[09:32] [00:09:32] Alex: minor transcription hiccup - during the demo your slide showed "KV cahce" typo; but the concept was clear.
[09:38] Olivia: noted, we'll fix typos.
[09:40] Priya: please cc our security team on the docs.
[09:43] Samir: will do.
[09:45] [00:09:45] Rachel: thanks everyone, that was really helpful.
[09:48] Samir: thanks all - we'll follow up with the artifacts. bye.
[09:52] [00:09:52] (meeting ends)
